extracted.intended_audience: State Departments of Transportation (State DOTs), Metropolitan Planning Organizations (MPOs), and other transportation agency implementers of FHWA performance measures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for establishing, reporting, and implementing the FHWA on-road greenhouse gas (CO2) performance measure on the National Highway System, including target-setting, reporting schedules, joint targets, and related data and documentation expectations for State DOTs and MPOs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the measure — total tailpipe CO2 on the NHS
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure addresses total tailpipe CO2 emissions on the National Highway System (NHS) rather than normalizing this value by population or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FHWA believes atmospheric CO2 concentrations are ultimately influenced by the total quantity of CO2 emissions produced; measuring total emissions supports a whole-of-government approach and provides a consistent measure at National, State, and metropolitan levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to establish declining targets
rubrics_metrics.description: State DOTs and MPOs are required under the rule to establish declining targets for reducing CO2 emissions generated by on-road mobile sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets must be declining but FHWA is not prescribing specific declining target levels; State DOTs and MPOs have flexibility to set targets appropriate for their communities and policy priorities. FHWA retained this requirement given the urgency of the climate crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targets are flexible; FHWA does not set or approve targets
rubrics_metrics.description: FHWA does not set or approve State DOT's or MPO's targets; State DOTs and MPOs have discretion in setting an appropriate declining target informed by complete, consistent, and timely State and local information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets should be informed by local data and analysis; FHWA rejects characterizations that the requirement forces specific project selection. The rule imposes no penalties on States and MPOs that do not meet their targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: No penalties for failing to meet targets
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no specific penalties for failing to achieve GHG targets; FHWA did not propose or finalize any penalties for failure to achieve performance targets for this measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If significant progress is not made, the State DOT must document the actions it will take to achieve that target no later than in its next biennial report (and is encouraged to do so sooner). Significant progress is described in 23 CFR 490.109; failure to achieve significant progress will not trigger penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and target-establishment schedule (timing requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: State DOTs will establish targets no later than February 1, 2024; MPOs must establish targets no later than 180 days after the State DOT establishes their targets. Targets will be established/adjusted every two years beginning in 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The GHG measure has a 4-year performance period beginning January 1, 2022. State reporting will follow an October 1 cycle beginning in 2026 to align with other measures. Because initial targets are established near the mid-point (2024), 2-year targets are not required for the initial cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Initial GHG Report content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: State DOTs must submit a State Initial GHG Report (by Feb 1, 2024) that provides the 4-year target, the basis for the target, the baseline data (reference year for the performance period), the relationship with other performance expectations, the data points used to calculate the GHG metric, and the value calculated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State Initial GHG Report requirements are similar to the Baseline Performance Period Report; the report provides the basis for target-setting and documents data used for the metric as specified in 23 CFR 490.107(d) and 490.511(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: MPO joint UZA targets requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: MPOs are required to collectively establish a single joint 4-year target for each Urbanized Area (UZA) that contains NHS mileage and that is overlapped by the boundaries of two or more metropolitan planning areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint UZA targets are required in addition to each MPO's individual metropolitan planning area target. FHWA retained the joint-target requirement to encourage collaboration across MPO boundaries and region-based approaches to reducing GHG emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targets must be quantifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint targets (and other targets) are required to be a quantifiable target, meaning a value must be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets should use a numeric value rather than qualitative descriptions to enable measurement and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: No required 8- and 20-year targets
rubrics_metrics.description: FHWA considered but declined to require long-term (8- and 20-year) targets in the final rule to remain consistent with the existing TPM framework used for other NHPP measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State DOTs and MPOs may voluntarily establish longer-term targets in a manner that aligns with their own policies and plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPO target frequency — retain 4-year targets
rubrics_metrics.description: FHWA retained the requirement for MPOs to establish 4-year targets; the agency declined to require additional 2-year targets or to change to 8- and 20-year-only targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FHWA determined that the benefits of additional target frequencies would not justify added burden or complexity; MPOs will report baseline performance and progress in their system performance reports per 23 CFR 490.107.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric data source and distinct purpose from other Federal programs
rubrics_metrics.description: FHWA's GHG measure specifically addresses CO2 from on-road activity and utilizes FHWA's fuel use data shortly after its publication; this is distinct from CAFE vehicle standards and EPA/DOE national emission estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FHWA's data are more timely and disaggregated for on-road activity, supporting transportation decision-making by accounting for VMT, congestion, and other on-road factors. The measure is intended to complement, not duplicate, other Federal programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of complete, consistent, and timely local information in target setting
rubrics_metrics.description: State DOTs and MPOs should use complete, consistent, and timely State and local information on GHG emissions from on-road mobile sources to inform target-setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FHWA expects data-driven target-setting using appropriate local projections and analyses. FHWA considered comments requesting that States provide underlying assumptions and rationale for vehicle emissions rates and VMT; while not prescribing a specific set of assumptions, FHWA indicated targets should be informed by projections for vehicle efficiency, VMT-reducing investments, system efficiency enhancements, and other strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of transportation agency actions and strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: FHWA recognizes transportation investments, vehicle electrification, highway operations, and roadway maintenance practices can influence travel behavior and reduce GHG emissions and that agencies have multiple strategies to reduce on-road CO2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may use Federal-aid funds and BIL programs (e.g., EV charging, transit, pedestrian/bicycle infrastructure, roadway operations) and other strategies (idle reduction, travel demand management, car/ride sharing) to influence emissions; FHWA rejects the premise that agencies have limited capacity to influence GHG emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of Federal funding to assist target achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: BIL provides funding (more than $27 billion across several programs) to help State DOTs and MPOs achieve GHG reduction targets, including formula funds and competitive grants for EV infrastructure, transit, and active transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FHWA cites specific funding programs (CRP, NEVI, competitive EV/alternative fuel infrastructure grants, Transportation Alternatives Set-Aside, transit funding) as resources agencies can leverage; the rule itself does not tie funding eligibility to target achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: FHWA technical assistance and tools expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: FHWA points to existing technical assistance, tools, and guidance available (TPM and Energy and Emissions websites, National Highway Institute, AASHTO, AAMPO) and launched an Every Day Counts innovation to help quantify GHG emissions and set targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FHWA will continue to consider how best to support State DOTs and MPOs in implementing TPM requirements and will provide ongoing technical assistance; commenters requested additional tools such as modeling best practices, strategies/pathways to reduce CO2, and guidance on factors to consider in setting targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: No exemptions for rural States or attainment areas
rubrics_metrics.description: FHWA declines to exempt rural States, States with rapidly growing populations, or areas in attainment with National Ambient Air Quality Standards from the GHG measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FHWA reasoning: GHGs are global and emitted everywhere; rural States contribute to atmospheric CO2 and have alternative strategies (EV infrastructure, roadway operations, asset management) and funding sources to reduce emissions. Exemptions would run counter to the rule's purpose of providing consistent information about on-road mobile emissions on the NHS.

rubrics_metrics.name: FHWA cannot impose incentives/disincentives that restrict use of Federal funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 23 U.S.C. 145, the Federal-aid highway program is federally assisted and State-administered; FHWA does not have authority to broadly limit use of transportation funds or restrict funding for States that fail to meet targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters' recommendations to provide extra points in grants or restrict funds for noncompliance exceed FHWA authority; however, BIL includes new programs that may help States and MPOs fund projects that reduce GHG emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: If significant progress is not made, required documentation of actions
rubrics_metrics.description: If significant progress is not made for the target established for the GHG measure, the State DOT must document the actions it will take to achieve that target no later than in its next biennial report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The documentation requirement is consistent with existing NHPP performance measures; the State is encouraged to document actions sooner. Significant progress is further described in 23 CFR 490.109.

rubrics_metrics.name: FHWA will not provide intermediate national benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: FHWA declines to provide intermediate benchmarks for States to ensure they are on track to meet the 2030 national GHG reduction goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While FHWA removed the requirement to align targets with national goals or provide benchmarks, State DOTs and MPOs may voluntarily establish longer-term targets to serve as intermediate benchmarks aligned with long-term GHG reduction goals.
